case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old girl presented to an outpatient clinic with a history of a red plaque on her chest for over 4 years. Her parents first noticed the asymptomatic, round red lesion, approximately 3 mm in diameter, when she was 2 years old. The lesion had well-defined borders, a smooth surface, and visible dilated blood vessels. She was evaluated at a local hospital at the time, diagnosed with a birthmark, and no treatment was administered. However, the lesion gradually enlarged and became slightly sunken. The girl was conceived through in vitro fertilization and was vaginally delivered at term. She had no other significant medical or family history. Upon physical examination, a slightly sunken red plaque was observed on the chest, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, with a smooth surface, associated vascular dilation, well-defined borders, and no scaling or ulceration (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed from the edge of the plaque.
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of a slightly sunken red plaque on the chest. B, Histopathology reveals significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

dialogue_history.speaker: medical
dialogue_history.text: I disagree with the diagnosis of atrophic dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) here. In a child, a long-standing, slowly enlarging, sunken red plaque with visible vessels is far more characteristic of a benign vascular lesion like a congenital hemangioma involuting or an atrophic capillary malformation, not an aggressive spindle-cell tumor. While spindle cells can be seen in DFSP, its presentation in early childhood is exceptionally rare, and the described history and morphology strongly favor a vascular origin.

metadata.belief: The lesion is most likely a benign vascular anomaly, such as an involuting congenital hemangioma or an atrophic capillary malformation/nevus, rather than a dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
metadata.reasoning: The patient's age, lesion duration, and clinical features are classic for a benign vascular lesion, not an aggressive sarcoma typically seen in adults.

dialogue_history.text: While I acknowledge the rarity of atrophic dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in young children, the histopathology showing significant proliferation of spindle cells arranged in a bandlike distribution is quite suggestive of this diagnosis. The lesion's long-standing nature and gradual enlargement do not exclude DFSP, which can have a benign appearance initially. We should remain vigilant for its potential local aggression, and further management should still prioritize surgical evaluation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Her parents first noticed the asymptomatic, round red lesion, approximately 3 mm in diameter, when she was 2 years old. The lesion had well-defined borders, a smooth surface, and visible dilated blood vessels. She was evaluated at a local hospital at the time, diagnosed with a birthmark, and no treatment was administered. However, the lesion gradually enlarged and became slightly sunken. The girl was conceived through in vitro fertilization and was vaginally delivered at term. She had no other significant medical or family history. Upon physical examination, a slightly sunken red plaque was observed on the chest, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, with a smooth surface, associated vascular dilation, well-defined borders, and no scaling or ulceration (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed from the edge of the plaque.
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of a slightly sunken red plaque on the chest. B, Histopathology reveals significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old girl presented to an outpatient clinic with a history of a red plaque on her chest for over 4 years. Her parents first noticed the asymptomatic, round red lesion, approximately 3 mm in diameter, when she was 2 years old. The lesion had well-defined borders, a smooth surface, and visible dilated blood vessels. She was evaluated at a local hospital at the time, diagnosed with a birthmark, and no treatment was administered. However, the lesion gradually enlarged and became slightly sunken. The girl was conceived through in vitro fertilization and was vaginally delivered at term. She had no other significant medical or family history. Upon physical examination, a slightly sunken red plaque was observed on the chest, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, with a smooth surface, associated vascular dilation, well-defined borders, and no scaling or ulceration (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed from the edge of the plaque.
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of a slightly sunken red plaque on the chest. B, Histopathology reveals significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

case_info.explanation: D. Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.

Plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma The pathological results indicated that the epidermis was generally normal, with significant proliferation of spindle cells in the superficial to mid-dermis, arranged in a bandlike distribution, without significant mitotic figures or cellular atypia. Additionally, there was considerable vascular proliferation in the stroma (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed strong positivity for CD34, scattered positivity for S100, and Ki67 positivity of less than 2%, while P63, desmin, and SMA were negative. Further fluorescence in situ hybridization testing was performed, yielding negative results for theCOL1A1/PDGFBfusion gene. Thus, the patient was ultimately diagnosed with plaquelike CD34-positive dermal fibroma (PDF) (Figure 2). Given that this condition is a benign skin tumor, we proceeded a standard excision for the patient, as opposed to wide local excision. PDF, also referred to as medallion-like dermal dendrocyte hamartoma, is a rare benign skin tumor. It was first reported by Rodríguez-Jurado et al1in 2004, describing this congenital, mildly atrophic reddish-brown lesion in 3 girls. The pathogenesis of PDF remains unclear and may be related to postzygotic mutation leading to cutaneous mosaicism.2Clinically, the typical presentation is a reddish or brown, round or oval plaque, approximately the size of a coin or larger, with slight atrophy or sclerosis; although rare presentations include skin-colored papules3or subcutaneous nodules.4 Histopathologically, PDF is characterized by bandlike infiltration of spindle fibroblasts in the superficial and mid-dermis, surrounded by dense collagen fibers, with fragmented or reduced elastic fibers. The lesion is rich in blood vessels and may occasionally extend into the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemical staining reveals strong CD34 positivity, with some tumor cells also co-expressing factor XIIIa. The differential diagnosis includes spindle cell tumors, particularly lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor (LPF-NT), fibroblastic connective tissue nevus, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). LPF-NT is a rare soft tissue tumor that primarily occurs in children and young adults. Histologically, it is typically characterized by infiltrative proliferation of spindle cells within subcutis.5Recently, a dermal subtype has been reported, which mainly involves the entire dermis with minimal involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.6The proliferative cells in LPF-NT are positive for CD34, S100, and NTRK1, which aids in distinguishing it from PDF. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus is a benign skin mesenchymal tumor belonging to the connective tissue nevus spectrum, characterized by solitary, ill-defined, slowly growing and painless plaques or nodules and primarily seen in young female individuals younger than 10 years. The distinction lies mainly in the histopathology showing spindle cell proliferation in the deep dermis, arranged in intersecting fascicular patterns. Immunostaining typically shows weak positivity for CD34 and SMA, while desmin and S100 protein are negative.7DFSP is a rare, low-grade malignant soft tissue dermal tumor, which clinically presents as slowly growing skin-colored plaques without significant symptoms, and gradually develops into purple or reddish-brown nodules. It is often overlooked due to its gradual, localized infiltrative growth. There are various clinical and histological subtypes, among which the atrophic type is a rare variant, characterized by slightly atrophic, painless, indurated dark red plaques.8The atrophic variants of DFSP and PDF are very similar in their clinical manifestations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. However, DFSP requires wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery because it is a locally aggressive, low-grade sarcoma with a risk of metastasis (although rare), and complete excision with clear margins is essential to reduce the chance of recurrence. Due to the presence of the chromosomal translocation t (17;22) (q22; q13) in more than 90% of DFSP,9further fluorescence in situ hybridization  analysis is required to detect the presence of the fusion geneCOL1A1/PDGFBto differentiate DFSP from PDF.10 It is important to differentiate PDF from some CD34-positive spindle cell tumors since PDF is a benign tumor that typically does not recur after surgical excision; in this case, the patient has shown no signs of recurrence during follow-up.
